newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain poised to soften inflation target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain poised to soften inflation target.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government looked set on Thursday to soften its stand on inflation by telling the Bank of England not to squeeze the economy too much with higher interest rates.

Three leading British newspapers said that in a keynote speech on Thursday night, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown would keep the long-standing 2.5 percent underlying annual inflation target as his central objective.
But they said that instead of setting the target at "2.5 percent or less," Brown would impose penalties on the Bank of England if inflation was one percentage point above or below the target.
The intention would be to ensure that the Bank, newly empowered by Brown to set interest rates, successfully fought inflation but did not damage the economy by raising interest rates too much.
City economists said that if the reports on Brown's Mansion House speech in the City of London were correct, it suggested a softer monetary policy.
"This would represent a diminution of the toughness of monetary policy," said Ian Stewart, economist at Merrill Lynch.
"The current target, effectively a band between zero and 2.5 percent, is bring replaced by a higher band of 1.5 to 3.5 percent."
However, Marion Bell, an economist at Royal Bank of Scotland, said measures of this sort could prevent the central bank from being over-zealous in fighting inflation.
"At present there is nothing to stop the Bank being too tight and causing lots of unemployment and falling output in order to get falling prices," she told ITN television.

The Treasury declined to comment on the reports in the Financial Times, the Guardian and the Telegraph. They said that if inflation was more than one percentage point off target, Bank of England Governor Eddie George would have to write an open letter to Brown explaining the reasons.
George would have to outline what actions the Bank was taking to correct the situation and predict when inflation would be back on track.
Stewart said amending the target in the way suggested by the newspaper reports would imply the government was prepared to tolerate inflation between 2.5 and 3.5 percent.
Under the present system, the Bank misses its target if underlying inflation is 0.25 percentage points above the target, but is deemed to have hit it if inflation is 0.25 percentage points below.

Underlying inflation -- which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments -- remained at the 2.5 percent target set by the previous Conservative government in May, according to official figures released on Thursday.
It first dipped to this level in April.
City analysts questioned the timing of the change.

"It is rather strange to soften the inflation target at this stage of the experiment," said Stewart, referring to the fact that the Bank of England was given freedom to set interest rates only weeks five weeks ago.
"It would have been more sensible to try and build credibility in the new system."
The Bank's new monetary policy committee raised interest rates at the first opportunity last Friday to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent.
Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers, said the Bank would probably now go out of its way to emphasise it was aiming for inflation at 2.5 percent and not just the top of the wider band.
"If this band is considered acceptable, I think it will go down very badly in financial markets," he said.
The suggested band implied that the costs of having inflation under 1.5 percent were the same as the costs of having it above 3.5 percent.
"That is clearly not the case and it will make for a very poor comparison with other European economies," said Dicks.
British government bonds shrugged off the newspaper reports and were firm on Thursday morning. The September gilt future was up 6/32 at 113-25.
